I would like to bring a certain matter to the attention of the government. Recently there has been reported the absorption of the Famous Players Canadian Corporation by the Paramount Famous Lasky Corporation of America, and I find that there has been a great deal of discussion about it. I have in my hand the Canadian Moving Picture Digest which contains very extensive editorials and comments of one kind and another in regard to this absorption. I shall read one or two extracts. One of them refers to the Canadian company as being the dominant theatre chain in the Dominion; it states that the Famous Players Canadian Corporation is distinctly a Canadian concern and financed by Canadian shareholders. In part, the editorial is as follows:
The Famous Players Canadian Corporation if sold to an American company, gives that company a film monopoly in Canada which is worth at least $100,000,000.
I wish to make another observation which represents my right to ask the question. In view of the prospectus issued to the public in March of 1929 wherein it was stated that voting trust certificates were listed on the Toronto and Montreal stock exchanges, and wherein Canadian control of the company was assured to Canadian shareholders, I wish to ask if the government has been apprised of the circumstances connected with the sale of the Famous Players Canadian Corporation to the Paramount Famous Lasky Corporation and if any action has been taken in connection therewith, or whether any action has been proposed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY COMMISSION TO BEATTY COMMISSION EXTENDING INQUIRY TO SERVICE GENERALLY
speechtext:
I seek as much as possible
to avoid raising questions of privilege. However, at least once in every parliament it 2419-137
seems neeessary to make a statement about some article which appears in the Ottawa Journal. This morning the following appears on the editorial page:	It is entitled "A
Promise, and a Performance":
On September 13, 1926, Mr. Mackenzie King stood in the Ottawa auditorium and addressing an audience composed largely of Ottawa civil servants, made this statement:
Then follows the statement in quotations:
"Last year, I recall we passed an order in council referring to the Civil Service Commission, the whole question of the revision of civil servants' salaries. We referred it to that body because, under a law which was passed prior to our coming into office, the Civil Service Commission was the body which had to do with the regulating of the salaries of civil servants. We made certain requests in the order in council as to the basis on -which a revision should be made. When we got the report of the commission it was not satisfactory, either to the government or the civil service. Having had representations from the service in regard to it we referred it back again to the commission."
The quotation continues with the following sentence in italics:
"Now I wish to say that if we are returned to power I intend to use what influence I can to see that the salaries are revised in accordance with the instructions given in the order in council."
The editorial continues:
That was three days before the last general election; Ottawa civil servants took Mr. King to mean what he said, helped return him to power.
On Wednesday, exactly four years after the foregoing pledge. Mr. King arose in the House of Commons and said this:
"So far as the government is concerned I may say we are giving very careful attention to the whole question of what is to be done *with regard to the salaries of members of the public service."
The comment of the newspaper on that statement follow's in the editorial and is as follows:
No need exists to comment upon what is revealed by these two statements made four years apart. They can be left to the intelligence of Ottawa civil servants themselves.
Mr. Speaker, any person reading that article would be led to believe that I had made a promise on the eve of an election with respect to the salaries of civil servants, that in the interval nothing had been done, and that four years later in speaking again of the salaries of civil servants I had been making reference to the same matter. As a matter of fact, when parliament met after the general election at the very first session this government asked parliament for an increase for civil servants to implement the promise made at that time, and to carry out exactly what was stated i*

2162	COMMONS
Civil Service-Beatty Commission
my remarks at the Auditorium as quoted. If hon. members wish the record they will find it in Hansard of April 14, 1927. At the very first session which was the earliest opportunity, the government in the estimates as tabled placed an amount of $2,700,000 "to provide for flat increases to the civil service, both inside and outside." The hon. the Secretary of State was dealing with this estimate on the 14th of April and made a statement with reference to this flat increase. I shall not read all that he said, but to make clear exactly how the increase related to the service I might quote from Hansard his words in part. They will be found at page 2506:
When this item was called last night I proceeded to give an explanation of the proposed salary revision but I acceded to the request of one hon. member opposite that I defer until to-day any statement that I wished to make, in order that it might be presented to a full house.
Then the Secretary of State went on to say:
The proposal now' before the committee is based on the principle of a flat increase to the different classes of the service in receipt of salaries up to $5,100.
Then a little further on:
The proposal is of a dual nature. First it raises the minimum and maximum in every class of the service by the sum of $120 except in the case of the lowest minimum, that is, the entrant class. That has not been touched. Our reason for not increasing the lowest minimum was that entrants to the service are not affected and we thought we should not touch that minimum. This increase is not only for the present year but it is a permanent addition; so that every civil servant not only receives immediate consideration but has an increased maximum at which he may hope to arrive in the future. I might add there have been other increases as well.
_ Now, Mr. Speaker, those are the facts, and in the light of them if there is any inference to be drawn from my remarks of Wednesday last I submit that it is that when this government makes a promise to the civil servants or to any other body in this country, they may rely on that promise being carried out.
I went on to say on Wednesday that we were considering further the question of salaries of civil servants, and that we were considering the advisability of having the Beatty commission, which investigated the salaries of professional and technical members of the service, consider the service generally in accordance with a recommendation made by the commission in its report to the government. To-day we have asked His Excellency to give his assent, and it has been given to an order in council which will enable that step to be taken. The powers of the commission will be extended to include an examination
fMr Mackenzie King.]
into the question of the salaries of civil servants generally in accordance with the recommendation to which I have referred. We have also thought it desirable to have referred to that commission for consideration and report the advisability of fixing a minimum salary for employees of the civil service. I have in my hand the order in council which contains these two directions to the commission and I shall table it forthwith.

speechtext:
Certified to be a true copy of a minute of a meeting of the committee of the Privy Council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 16th May, 1930.
The committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 15th May, 1930, from the Secretary of State, submitting:
1.	That by order in council P.C. 664, dated 15th April, 1929, a Royal commission composed of: Edward W. Beatty, Esq., president of the Canadian Pacific Railway; Sir George Garneau, Quebec, and Dr. Walter C. Murray, LL.D., Saskatoon. was appointed to inquire into rates of salaries, pensions, etc., of technical and professional officials of the Civil Service of Canada.
2.	That by order in council P.C. 1195, dated 2nd July, 1929, the said royal commission was authorized to include within the scope of its enquiry the salaries of civil service commissioners, board of pension commissioners, railway commissioners and all officers having the rank of deputy ministers and also all such employees of the government whether subject to the Civil Service Act or not.
3.	That the said royal commissioners have submitted their report containing certain recommendations and suggestions among which is the following:
"27. Suggested further investigation of the civil service generally.
During the course of our inquiry, we were impressed with the fact that those engaged in technical, scientific and professional work for the government, though they formed a very important branch of the civil service, were still in numbers only a moderate proportion of the total engaged in government service. The cost of government, measured by salaries or wages alone, is substantial, and the number of employees very great. Having in mind the obvious desire of the government, as indicated by the reference to us, to improve the status of its technical officers with a view to increasing the efficiency of that branch of the service, it has occurred to us that an investigation of the civil service generally, i.e., as to numbers, nature of work and rates of pay, might conceivably result in some economy and greater efficiency. We are sensible of the fact that such a work is of considerable magnitude and would involve careful scrutiny of the personnel in each department, and that it would take a considerable time, but we believe the results would more than justify the expense of such an investigation. We appreciate, of course, that this is not a subject which has been referred to us. and that our observations are not strictly pertinent under the terms of the order in council, but the information adduced during the course of the inquiry has pointed so strongly to the possibility of an effective and valuable work being done in this way, in a further effort to improve the personnel and increase the efficiency in government service, that we felt we might, without impro-riety. suggest for the consideration of the government that at the appropriate time it might profitably be undertaken."
The minister further submits that in his opinion it is advisable that such investigation should be undertaken without delay: also that the advisability of fixing a minimum salary, for employees in the civil service should be considered.
2419-137i
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Secretary of State, advise that a supplementary commission be issued to the said commissioners extending the scope of the inquiry to include such investigation, and also the advisability of fixing a minimum salary for employees in the civil service.
E. J. Lemaire,
Clerk of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend misunderstands me. I did not say that it was a question whether or not the excise tax Should be included in calculating for duty purposes. I said, should it be regarded as automatically rendering the goods subject to dumping duty? That is a very different thing. The only change that is made is to get away from the situation which has existed since August 1, 1928, by which such goods, in addition to paying the duty, are automatically subject to dumping duty by reason of the existence of an excise tax in the country in which they are manufactured. In France, for instance, there is a sales or turn-over tax of 2 per cent; in Belgium, 1 per cent. In Belgium there is also a 6 per cent luxury tax which is limited in its application to certain articles. In Japan, 10 per cent on fixed values is the excise tax on silk. In Italy, there is a sales or turn-over tax of one-quarter of one per cent on raw materials and one-half of one per cent on manufactured products. Czechoslovakia has a 2 per cent sales or turnover tax and a 12 per cent luxury tax, limited in the range of articles to which it applies. In Spain there is a stamp tax on wines, the precise incidence of which has not been. worked out since August, 1928, when the change that we are now attempting to rectify came into effect. In Portugal the situation is very difficult on account of the sales or turnover tax being combined with the business profits tax. It is a matter of great difficulty to our customs people to know whether or not the dumping duty should apply to goods from Portugal because of the nature of their sales or turnover tax. Those are a few of the instances that I have been able to gather this morning, showing the complexity of the situation. There is no difficulty in connection with the levying of a straight duty. The difficulty is only in connection with adopting the principle that automatically goods are dumped because in the country of origin there is an excise tax.

I understand the minister's point now. He says he does not think it is fair that this excise tax should be considered when the dumping duty is applied. But the question in my mind is, what is the practical effect of this new clause so far as our own industries are concerned? Therefore it seems to me that the essential principle should be to determine what rate of duty on any particular commodity is reasonably necessary to meet the conditions surrounding the production of that commodity in our own land. The governments of the past have adopted as a practical policy that those productive activities of this country which afford remunerative employment to our people

A countervailing duty is undoubtedly a dealer's measure. It protects only the dealer, and it operates every time at the expense of the consumer. We will say, for instance, that when there is a glut on the American market they will at once raise their duty on foodstuffs. That might apply to meats. In conformity with the terms of the countervailing duty Canada's tariff rate must go up in order to meet that of the United States. That does not prevent the passage of meats across the border from one country to another because prices to the consumer go up in each country. However, it does give the dealer in each country a chance to fleece the consumer, and to my mind that is the effect that the countervailing duty will have upon the Canadian consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Speaking of this specific item, I cannot agree with my hon. friend when he describes the effect it will have upon the consumer in this country. Canada produces vast quantities of meats, and she exports those meats in competition with the world. As we develop-as I hope and believe we will-a greater cooperative effort for the disposal of those meats, the countervailing duties in connection with fresh meats certainly will not have the effect of raising the price to the consumer.

There has been practically no relationship between the price paid to the farmer and the price the consumer has had to pay the retail stores. That is very largely due to the control of prices by the packers of this country, and this measure will give them greater opportunity to fix their own prices. A countervailing duty cannot be effective in the interests of any country or the interests of the general public unless it comes down to freer trade. It is entirely a dealer's measure, and advantage will be taken by those controlling the supply. We have not taken advantage of countervailing duties when we have been offered free trade. For many years the United States has been offering us free trade in coal. We have never taken advantage of the offer but have chosen to put a duty on our coal, which the consumer has had to pay. Countervailing duties on meats,

eggs and any other commodities will always operate against the interests of the consumer. I wish to say that my hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan) was quite right, despite his party blindness; it would seem that at times he talks in the interests of the general public. There is no doubt that these countervailing duties will raise the cost of living in this country, especially in view of the fact that the packers will have control of prices. Duties will go up in both countries when" the supply is in the hands of those packers. Where the local market can be controlled by local supplies the prices may be more regular, but once the supply becomes greater than the local market can handle the price will go up because it is controlled by the packers.

speechtext: Yes, and we will come to that item presently.

Under this item I should
like to direct the attention of the minister to what I consider to be a grave omission from the list of items under the countervailing duties. I refer to fish, which I think should be included under this heading. If any hon. member questions me I can quote from the Bible, from Murray's classical dictionary and from Webster's new international dictionary to prove that fish is meat, and consequently should be included under this item. The fishing industry on the Pacific coast is very important, and I am quite sure that if a few facts are laid before the government they will realize the importanace of including fish under the countervailing tariff.
Here is the situation. At the present moment on the Pacific coast over 315 American vessels are engaged in the halibut trade, and they use Canadian ports without paying any dues at all. There are no harbour dues; they have the full freedom of those ports and they pay only 81 for a fishing licence. They have the full benefit of our railways in order to send their products to the American market, and they are able to get for their fresh fish 2 cents per pound more than the Canadian fisherman gets.
Why?

There is a duty of 2 cents per pound imposed on Canadian fish entering the United States. The result is that the Canadian fisherman is penalized to the extent of 2 cents a pound on his fish. If, on a stormy day, a Canadian fisherman should be unable to reach the' port of Prince Rupert and should turn into the port of Ketchikan, which is seventy miles north in United States territory, he has to pay poft dues, entrance and clearing charges, and' other things which cost a considerable sum, varying in respect of the size of the vessel. The point I should like to bring strongly to the attention of the minister is this: Why should not the Canadian fishermen be protected in accordance with the principle laid down by the countervailing duty which the government is applying to other commodities? Is he not entitled at least to have that protection which has been afforded
other industries such as agriculture? I have under my hand correspondence from many quarters; from the senator representing Alaska; from the report of the United States tariff commission; from the Seattle Fishermen's Association and from the Canadian Halibut Union, and all are agreed that a reasonable solution is possible. Until now we could not get the government to believe that when we advocated something for the relief of the Canadian Pacific fishermen we were not urging retaliation against the United States. That myth is dead; there is no more heard of it now, only I trust that the government will see to it that this very important industry is given relief. It is only what is coming to it and is in accord with the principle which has been laid down under the item now under discussion. Without saying anything further, I hope this matter will receive the immediate attention of the Minister of Finance and that he will add this one item to the present list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course I shall be very glad to consider anything advanced by my hon. friend, but I would respectfully refer him to the wholesale condemnation of the countervailing idea as expressed by his colleague from St. Lawrence-St. George.
But could you not do something in the way of some landing tax which would give relief to our Canadian fishermen?

When these ships come in loaded with their fish is it not an advantage to your ports? Do they not buy the packages in which the fish are shipped, and the ice which is put up by your own workmen? Do not the Canadian railroads carry those fish from your ports to the United States? Do not your ports get vast advantages out of that situation?

That is conceded; they buy their ice there, and no doubt the railways receive substantial profits from that traffic. We desire to have them receive those profits, and we welcome the American fishermen to our port. But the American fisherman who enters our ports is not permitted by his government to have any repairs done, nor can he except in a limited degree purchase any supplies at that port; he must do that in United States territory. In other words, he sells his fish on the exchange in competition with Canadian fishermen at a price 2 cents per pound above that received by the Canadian fisherman, and gets the full benefits of the port. I think it will be agreed that some right lies on the side of Canadian fishermen,

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
because he is asking only for a fair and equitable agreement.
Prince Rupert is the only harbour on the Pacific coast which meets the requirements of the large American fishing fleet. Ketchikan has no railway connection to the United States market. Last year there were landed in Prince Rupert 30,500,000 pounds of halibut, of which the Canadians sold about 3,750,000 pounds to the United States. If the American fishermen were not permitted to enter Prince Rupert harbour, they would be forced to travel often nearly 1,200 miles to Seattle, and that would be a difficult and dangerous voyage in bad weather even for the larger boats. The Canadian fisherman asks that the provision which is to be applied to other industries should be applied to the third greatest industry in Canada; he asks that this industry be given a fair chance.

The explanation given by the hon. member might apply to certain conditions prevailing in British Columbia, but I would like to hear from some of the hon. members from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

What are the Americans doing on the Atlantic seaboard? A Canadian fishing vessel on the Atlantic seaboard cannot enter an American port in order to sell its fish; it must return to a Canadian port and transfer the fish into carriers for disposal in United States markets. What is being done in Prince Rupert? American vessels to the number of over 300 enter the port without paying anything, the fish is sold on the exchange in competition with Canadian fish, put into bond and given quick transit into the United States. This question has never been brought by the government before the United States in the right manner, and I do honestly believe that the United States government will assist in a correct settlement of this problem, one which would give to the Canadian halibut fisherman that which he is entitled to. The port of Prince Rupert and the Canadian fishermen should be treated on an equitable basis, especially when one considers that the United States is considering the raising of the duty on frozen halibut to 5 cents per pound.
We have been hearing of Japan in connection with silk, but let us consider that country from a fishing standpoint. Last year the Japanese landed in the city of Seattle 400,000 pounds of very excellent frozen halibut, which was sold at 9 cents per pound, which price included the 2 cents per pound duty. Let us 
suppose that the rate suggested by the United States tariff board goes into effect-what might happen? Japan -would immediately turn her attention to Canada and it would not be very long before a serious situation might exist here. The Japanese can catch the fish, bring them across the Pacific to Seattle, and sell them for 9 cents per pound. Would the Canadian fisherman, operating a five-man boat, be able to compete with the Japanese?

It is the little things which swing the pivot or change the flow of commerce.
I think I have placed squarely before the finance minister and the government the desire of the Canadian fishermen, namely, to get justice in their fair demands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friends have been condemning those countervailing duties; they said that that would be a made-in AVashington policy.
Put a straight duty on then, or a port tax.

That is the only thing you
offer us, so how can we go after you for anything else? The hon. member for Skeena is quite right in the position he takes. The fishing industry in this country would be in a much better position had we a department of fisheries capable of handling the affairs of the industry. If laws were enacted governing the landing of fish in British Columbia, we would soon find the American fishermen offering us some concessions on the Atlantic. The American fishing vessels are allowed to use our ports without any restrictions; they can enter the port, land their cargoes and transport to the United States, but our vessels cannot enter an American port, even upon the payment of the duty of 2 cents per pound. If we want to send fish to the United States they must be landed at a Canadian port and transhipped into a regular carrier.

They do, but under certain restrictions.
Those restrictions do not exist on the Pacific coast?

They do not exist on the
Pacific coast at all.
That is what I wanted to find out from the minister.

A United States boat cannot come into one of our Atlantic ports and purchase bait and other supplies, but United States vessels can do this on the Pacific coast. That is where we have a lever. If we had a business administration handling the affairs of the Fisheries department, they would have looked into the matter long ago and used that lever with the United States. Then the United States would have been willing to give us concessions in regard to our markets for Atlantic fish. That is the answer to that. I am quite in accord with what the hon. member for Skeena has said with reference to the fishing industry on the Pacific coast. If we would look after our own interests on the Pacific coast, we would have our United States friends offering us entirely different terms with reference to our Atlantic fish.

The question which has
been brought forward by the hon. member for Skeena is really worthy of every consideration. I do not want to rebuke the minister, but I think he treated in a rather light manner what was a very fair and courteous presentation, and I notice that some of his supporters rather laughed at the proposal. Let us look at the matter frankly for a moment and let me supplement what the hon. member for Skeena has most ably and courteously put forward. In the Pacific ocean there is a great fishing area inside and outside of territorial waters. The United States fishermen come north from Seattle and fish outside the territorial waters in international waters. They have in the United States no place where they can properly handle that fish. AAre extend to them without any interference whatever all the courtesies that are extended to a Canadian fishing boat. They bring their fish into Prince Rupert and by virtue of that privilege, a strictly Canadian privilege, which is extended to them, they are enabled to ship about 27,000,000 pounds of halibut a year, chiefly to the New England market, as against 3,000,000 pounds that Canadian fishermen are able to fish into that market. AVhy cannot the Canadian fishermen ship as much as the United States fishermen? For the very simple reason that the United States impose a duty of two cents a pound on the fish which they handle and can handle only through Canadian facilities. That has been going on year after year. The point is this: the hon. member for Moose Jaw a moment ago asked a question -and I have no criticism to make of the form of it-did not Prince Rupert, a Canadian city, benefit from United States vessels coming in there? Certainly it did to a meagre extent; Prince Rupert under necessity endures that condition, but it would very much rather have Canadian fleets coming in and have the full supplying of those vessels. The United States vessels do not buy their supplies in Prince Rupert. They may buy ice; they may buy some supplies that are absolutely necessary, but they slip along the coast to Ketchikan, which has developed into quite a city through supplying these very boats. But Ketchikan is so situated geographically that it cannot serve in other ways the fishermen whom it supplies. Therefore Prince Rupert is left, to use a slang phrase, holding the sack. In other words, out of this vast fishing industry-and it is vast, because 30,000,000 pounds of one class of fish, namely, halibut, is a considerable quantity-Prince Rupert is taking perhaps one-fifth of what it ought to be getting, or less than that.

Certainly a very meagre portion of what it is entitled to. For years our United States friends have imposed this rather onerous duty, because two cents a pound on large quantities of fresh fish is, as my hon. friends will realize, a somewhat stiff tariff. I agree with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis that our United States friends would be very much perturbed if they thought we were going to deny them these privileges which we have so freely extended to them. What we are doing is this, and I will just illustrate the point: the government . puts live hogs under the countervailing duty. This does not amount to anything. We get and can get no live hogs from Great Britain. Therefore this does not help Great Britain and it does not amount to much. But fish is a commodity that might be treated in this manner with some advantage to Canada, and that is what my hon. friend is suggesting. He, like the rest of us, would prefer that we talk very plainly to the people of the United States in this regard and put a straight duty on fish. I am not saying that that alone would correct the situation. We should do that and also notify them that we are not going to give them the facilities at one of our ports if they are going to treat the very product handled through that facility in a manner that keeps our people out of the market. I think the proposition was very fairly and well advanced by the hon. member for Skeena and it is a subject that merits the closest scrutiny by parliament and the government.

What is the reason for the difference between the treatment of United States vesels on the west coast and that on the east coast?
_ Mr- STEVENS: The history of the matter is long and intricate and I am not in a position offhand to answer the question, but from memory I would say this: for many years there has been a modus vivendi on the Atlantic coast. I brought the matter to the attention of parliament some years ago, and if I recall rightly,

at that price; it makes one wonder whether beef is being dumped in Canada or whether it is of a very low quality. If it is a low quality product and if it is not properly stamped so that the consumer will know what he is buying, the result will certainly be to hurt the beef trade in Canada, and diminish the demand for beef of any kind. At this time I shall quote some figures from a bulletin recently issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. It shows that on the 1st of February, 1930, we had in storage 7,100,107 pounds of frozen mutton and lamb. On the same date we had in storage 594,525 pounds of mutton and lamb, -not frozen. The frozen mutton and lamb in storage as of February 1 was 7,100,107 pounds as compared with a five year average of 4,827,251 pounds, showing an increase in the storage stock of 47.08 per cent. The mutton and lamb in storage, not frozen, was 594,525 pounds on February 1, 1930 as compared with a five-year average of 280,003 pounds, showing an increase of 112.33 per cent. In both frozen and fresh meats there was an increase shown of 50.66 per cent. Some hon. members may say that 7.000,000 pounids of frozen and fresh mutton would make very little difference to the price of lamb and mutton received by the Canadian producer, and that it would represent only one pound per capita. My contention, however, and the contention of the sheep raisers in the portion of the country which I represent, is that this tremendous quantity of

I am informed by the live stock branch of the Department of Agriculture that in that boat there were 31,650 carcasses of Iamb weighing
1.266.000	pounds. In addition there were
4.000	carcasses of beef from Australia weighing 2,400,000 pounds, and on that same ship there were 270 bales of wool weighing 81,000 pounds. I am very glad indeed that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has seen fit to apply these countervailing duties; while they do not have very much effect with regard to frozen meat coming from New Zealand and Australia, they will affect importations from the United States. During the past few weeks I have had scores of telegrams from the sheep growers of souith&m Alberta complaining that sheep and lambs were about to be exported from the states of Washington, Oregon, and even California into the Vancouver market.

In the same year we exported goods to the value of $9,615,000 of which over $7,000,000 went to the United Kingdom and $1,961,000 to the United States. It is rather absurd to have a duty of li cents per pound on importations from Great Britain on an article like this which we do not import at all but which we export to the extent of $7,000,000 per year.

You do not expect to
have any imports of this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We do not expect to
import any considerable quantity of these articles from Great Britain. It will be noticed that there is a considerable two-way trade as between the United States and this
[Mr. Chaplin.
Our imports from the United States were $1,960,000 and our exports amounted to $1,961,000. In this particular case it is proposed to apply the countervailing duty. Our proposal is that the rates shall be If cents per pound under the intermediate, and 2 cents per pound under the general tariff. The present United States duty on cured bacon is 2 cents per pound, and by the bill at present before the senate it is proposed to raise that to 3J cents per pound. The present duty on pork in brine is 2 cents per pound, and the senate bill proposes to raise that to 3i cents per pound. The present duty on salted pork is 2 cents per pound, and it is proposed to raise that to 3-J cents per pound. The present duty on salted meats is 20 per cent ad valorem, and a specific duty of 6 cents per pound is proposed. Beef, dried and smoked meats and sausages bear a 20 per cent ad valorem rate, and the proposal is to increase that to a specific rate of 6 cents per pound.

The minister had better

What is the purpose of these changes? Who is asking for them? Have they been discussed before the tariff board or any other board? Did the minister suggest them out of some wild flight of imagination? Or is the object to make it appear that we are giving Great Britain a preference when we are really not doing so; as we are giving a preference in respect of comodities in which she does not trade with us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will try to answer that again. I stated in the budget that out of the hundreds of items being dealt with, there were some fifty which were non-effective so far as imports from Great Britain were concerned ; that in many such cases it was patently absurd to impose a tariff against Great Britain. I stated also that some of those fifty items, by reason of their being made free, represented trade possibilities with Great Britain. This I regard as one of the changes which may result in a growth of trade. It is only a minor item; it does not amount to a great deal, but trade is made up of small things, and with the advantage in favour of Great Britain by making the item free and without imposing any heavier burden upon those in Canada who have to buy beeswax, it is quite conceivable and even probable this trade with Great Britain will grow to a certain extent. We brought in a small amount last year.

We produce in Quebec
enough beeswax to supply the local demand. Why, then, should we encourage importations from any other country in the world? In Canada we can raise bees and produce honey of a quality and quantity sufficient for all our needs.

speechtext: You will have a lot of monopolies if you do not have freedom of trade.
I should like to give the producers in this country the very best position possible in their own market.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-16. Eggs in the shell, per dozen:	British preferential tariff, 2 cents;
intermediate tariff, 2J cents; general tariff, 3 cents.
Provided that, if any country imposes upon eggs in the shell, produced in, and imported from, Canada rates of duty higher than are enumerated in this item, equivalent rates of duty shall be imposed upon such commodities entering Canada from such country.

I should like to get an
explanation from the minister about this item. This is just a counterpart of the last tariff. Let me call the attention of the committee to this:	there are three items on eggs. The
first one, the minister has not changed. They have had enough eggs from Great Britain, so they do not change it. Britain last year sold us $3,000 worth of eggs. On the other two items: " eggs, whole, egg-yolks or egg albumen, frozen, and so forth, the items that we buy largely from China and of which Britain in 1929 sold us 722,000 pounds at a value of $120,000, they raised the duty 100 per cent. That shows how scared they are of eggs. They raise that tariff 100 per cent on the item in which Britain has largely dealt with us, but in respect to the two items in which Britain has not dealt very much with us, in the one case they leave the duty as it is at present, and in the other they lower it. In other words, in order to encourage business with Great Britain they increase the duty 100 per cent on the item that Britain has largely dealt in with us and they lower the duty on the item in which she deals with us only to a very small extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend does
not intend to be fair.
I do not think the minister should say that. I am making a statement of the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not discussing the item under consideration. He is lumping together three items and is mak-

ing certain statements about them. All I ask is that we discuss the item now before the committee. I will attempt to give information in connection with it in the proper order, and when we come to the next item I will endeavour to do the best I can with respect to it. I think I can satisfy the members of the committee by proceeding in an orderly manner without making a political speech which I could just as easily make as my hon. friend. My hon. friend thinks it is the proper thing to make a political speech on every item. I am trying to be patient and to give the information required, but I do not want him to think because he is making a political speech on every item, that another hon. member could not do the same thing.

About three months ago the farmers in this section of Canada were getting about fifty cents a dozen for eggs. Overnight the price dropped to twenty-two cents. Why? Because of the fact that the United States dumped millions of dozens of eggs into this country and they are doing the same thing to-day. Our countervailing duties will not prevent their doing the same thing again because, as we all know, in the United States they have a tariff commission which can raise or lower the duty at will. What is to prevent the egg producers in the United States from going to their tariff commission and saying:	Here, drop your duty.
Automatically ours goes down and then millions and millions of dozens of eggs will flow into this country as they have done before. There is in this budget a great defect which I feel the farmers should take cognizance of, because after all the poultry industry is really one that is of great value to Canada.

I have been consistently
opposing any increase in the tariff on eggs. I do this for various reasons. The first is that I do not believe a tariff on eggs will be of any benefit to the men who are producing eggs. During the past few years eggs have been bringing a fairly good price, and as a result of that Canada has now reached a point where she is producing practically as many eggs as she consumes. According to the figures given in the hearing before the tariff board, our exports of eggs for 1929 amounted to about 1,147,000 dozens and our imports amounted to about 713,000 dozens. Those figures show conclusively that we are reaching the point where we produce practically as many eggs as we consume. I am going to make a statement which I believe, and I think most of us believe is correct, namely, that when any product is on an export basis the tariff will not materially affect the price

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
to the producer. Tariffs increase the price of manufactured goods because the production of manufactured products can be controlled and the production of farm products cannot be controlled. Therefore tariffs do not generally increase prices to the producer. I am not going to labour that point because it has been made clear in the house several times already.
Does the hon. member mean agricultural products?

Yes, agricultural products or any products over the production of which you have no control. The United States endeavoured to increase the price of eggs, I suppose, in that country by raising the duty. I have here a clipping, one of several, showing the price of eggs in various markets. Tt is dated March 10, 1930, and shows that the price of extras in Toronto was 29 to 30 cents a dozen; Montreal, extras, 34 cents a dozen; New York, extras, 28 to 28^ cents a dozen. I think this shows conclusively that the high tariff of the United States is not having the effect of keeping the price of their eggs above the world's market price.
I have another reason for believing that a tariff on eggs is not in the best interests of the farmer. Unlike some other members of the house, I have a little sympathy for the consumer. We have been getting a fairly satisfactory price for our eggs as a general rule, and what the farmers are more interested in than a tariff on eggs is to get more commodities in exchange for the eggs they have to dispose of. I listened with a great deal of interest this afternoon to my hon. friend from Lincoln, with others, pleading that a 35 per cent tariff against the material that enters into the manufacture of artificial silk products was not sufficient to keep that industry alive in Canada. He apparently had received many communications from the manufacturers-

If my hon. friend will
allow me to interrupt him, I never spoke of artificial silk either last night or to-day-not one word.

Apparently the hon. member is not accountable for all he says. I gathered from the discussion this afternoon that the duty on artificial silk was 35 per cent, and my hon. friends were complaining that the changes under discussion were going to mean less profit for the manufacturers. I would like to know how many requests the hon. member for Lincoln has had from the employees in these factories who are wearing artificial silk, artificial silk stockings and other
such goods. What the farmer is interested in to-day is to get more for his dozen eggs when he trades them for other commodities than he has been getting in the past. We trade eggs for commodities largely, and what we want is more boots, more clothing or other products for the eggs we have to sell. I maintain that the tariff will not help the farmer. That is my stand.
This question was discussed before the tariff board, and I have read very carefully the evidence presented there. I am convinced that there was no case made out to warrant an increase in the tariff on eggs. I wish to quote a short extract from a letter written by the gentleman who presented this case before the tariff board. It is dated May 9, 1929, and says:
The poultry producers of western Canada are not requesting protection for the purpose of inflating the price of eggs to the consumer.
That sounds familiar.
They desire protection because they believe that the best interests of the producer and the consumer can only be protected by a stabilized market.
That sounds familiar too.
They wish to protect the distributors who purchase large quantities during the period of over-production, and who place them in store in order to protect the consumer from overinflation during the period of low production.
I have not a great deal of sympathy for the man who is gambling in eggs, who stores them up at one season of the year and unloads them at another. It is such concerns, apparently, that the writer of this letter refers to and is tlying to protect. The consumer in the city is paying from 55 to 60 cents a dozen for the eggs for which the producer in the country receives 30 to 40 cents a dozen, and I know of cases where the consumer is paying almost double what the producer within a hundred miles of the city receives.
At the same time of the year?

Yes, on the very same day. I maintain that that is one of the big difficulties so far as the producer is concerned. We are endeavouring to rectify that as fast as we can. Without detaining the house any further, or labouring the question, I am firmly convinced that that is where the great trouble lies, and I do not believe that increasing the tariff is going to be of any value to the producer of eggs in western Canada.

Would the hon. gentleman mind giving me his view, for my own in-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
formation, as to whether we should have such institutions as storage plants for carrying eggs over from the season of high production to the season of low production?
Most certainly.
It costs money to do that, of course.

I do not like to be
making the same objection to every item, but I am extremely glad to find that there is somebody in this house who is raising his voice on behalf of the ultimate consumer.
We are all consumers.
We all eat, don't we?

Eggs were selling last
year in Calgary at from 60 to 65 cents a dozen. Surely that is high enough without raising the price higher by means of a protective tariff, if that is the object. Certainly that is hoped to be the result of every tariff increase. My hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre in his address on the budget said that the United States had gone tariff mad. It seems to me that we are following in their footsteps, and if they have gone tariff mad, we too seem to be going tariff mad. I should like to ask the minister if, under this item, when the price of eggs comes down in the United States, the countervailing duty will come down also; because I can name a few articles on which our tariff is higher than that of the United States. If you believe in countervailing duties, why not make the two equal in all respects, and, where their tariff is lower than ours, reduce ours to the same level? I raise these objections as to the cost of living for the benefit of consumers generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was, as members of the committee know, a hearing of the Tariff Advisory Board with respect to this matter, and I think I should say that the application for an increase came from the Saskatchewan Cooperative Poultry Producers, otherwise known as the egg and poultry pool, and also from the Canadian Poultry Pool, Limited. In their reference they state that the organization comprises within its membership provincial poultry organizations of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and through them represents a membership of approximately 40,000 producers.
Would the minister read what Mr. Landreth said as to the number of dealers represented?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. He said:
I would like to add here that through the
2,000	merchant members we serve in the neighbourhood of another 200,000 poultry producers in the prairie provinces, that is regarding the merchants, large and small, as having 100 customers each, because under our merchants' contracts the merchants who belong to the pool agree to deliver all their eggs to the association. In that way we serve the producers of that area, although not contracted directly to the pool.
I was not discussing the nature of the constitution of the pool, I am not familiar with that detail. I was simply indicating that evidently a substantial number of those engaged in the poultry business were behind this application coming from the province of my hon. friend who has just spoken, Manitoba. I just wanted to give that information by way of showing that this matter was not handled in the dark at all, but that all the arguments were published; and while I know there is a difference of opinion between groups of farmers with respect to the matter, nevertheless these organizations are largely farmers' marketing organizations. I think no one can dispute that fact. They may have arrangements with the merchants that may modify their position as pool farmers, so to speak, but I know no reason to believe that they do not represent accurately the desires of their producer-members. I have had many representations from the producers' organizations, in fact they have come to see me upon the matter.
Did the minister get any representations from the Canadian Council of Agriculture or from the body of consumers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had no representations personally from the Canadian Council of Agriculture that I can recollect; but in this record of the tariff board hearings on the matter appears the opposition of the Canadian Council of Agriculture; that is, apparently they are opposed to the request of the egg pools of the various provinces. It is all on record in connection with the hearing.
Will the minister give us information as to the quantity of eggs imported in comparison with the number produced in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. There is a great variation in the imports in the various years. I will give the figures for the last five years:
Year	Value

These are our imports, chiefly from the United States, of eggs in the shell.

With regard to the application made before the tariff board, while it is perfectly true that it came from the organization of which the minister speaks, yet as a matter of fact the applicant was a Mr. Landreth, the general manager of one of these associations. I think I speak the absolute truth when I say that that man made the application without the consent and concurrence of the majority of the members of his organization, and I have had it repeated to me by those who attended the meetings when this matter was discussed and Mr. Landreth, in spite of what had been done, made the application. It came before the tariff board, and objection was then taken to it by the Consumers' League. The case was adjourned, and at the next hearing he did not appear; it was again adjourned, and he did not appear when it was called a third time, and again it was adjourned. I think on the fourth occasion he appeared, but there was no opportunity for the representative of the Canadian Council of Agriculture to appear because he was sick in bed. I am prepared to say that that application does not represent the opinion of the producers of eggs in western Canada. I am prepared also to say that it represents the opinions only of a very small minority, chiefly officials.
I do not think, as has already been pointed out by the member for Neepawa (Mr. Milne), that this tariff on eggs is likely to be of any benefit to the producers of eggs in western Canada. It is rather remarkable to find from the figures given by the minister that there has been a tremendous reduction in the importation of eggs during the past couple of years compared with what we imported in 1925. As a matter of fact, if my figures are correct as I got them from the minister, last year our importations were about a third of those of 1925.
Yesterday I said I would protest against the tariff on butter, eggs, fruit and vegetables, because I am absolutely convinced that the imposition of a tariff on these commodities is of no benefit to us in western Canada as producers, and certainly it will militate against any future activity of our farmer organizations to relieve themselves of the burdens that they have to bear by reason of the tariff. Therefore I am protesting against the imposition of this tariff on eggs.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask if the minister is aware of the fact that during the months of February and March there came into the city of Montreal from the United States one carload of eggs each week. Is he aware that during the early 2419-139
part of February when our farmers were getting 50 cents a dozen for their eggs, these importations over night caused the price to be cut in two? We in this country must realize that agriculture comes before all things.
Hear, hear.
We must realize that the farmer is the backbone of our country.
Why do you want to put such a heavy load on him?

Because we want to carry him on. We are anxious to put the farmer in the same position as some of our other producers have been in for many years. Let me tell you that the poultry raiser in Canada is entirely opposed to anything that will militate against the products of his poultry.

Has the minister the export
figures for the same years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. Canada exported whole eggs to a value of 1319,000 of which $264,000 went to the United Kingdom and $45,000 to Newfoundland.
What year was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For the fiscal year 1929.
Has the minister the figures for the two or three previous years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at the moment, but I can find them.

I think the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) takes a somewhat limited view of the expression "western Canada." Surely he will confine that term to his own province or to that and the one immediately beside it. I think I am entitled to have some say on the statement that the whole of western Canada has no desire for legislation of this character.
I will exclude British Columbia.

But he oanmot do that; we are in Canada, although we are too often neglected when the interests of the west are concerned. Some people seem to think that the west begins in Winnipeg and ends in the Rocky mountains, but geographically and politically that is not so. It has been suggested that Mr. Landreth, appearing before the tariff board on behalf of the Canadian egg pool, exceeded his authority. But the egg pool is the biggest organization of egg producers in the Dominion, and it would surely be a very anomalous position to find the recently appointed head of it arrogating to himself

2194	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
authority to decide what sort of fiscal policy his constituents want against their wishes. I would point out that the application was before the tariff board for a year or more, as the hon. gentleman behind me said, so there was ample time for the egg producers to express themselves if they were not in agreement with the application. Further than that, this application did not originate with Mr. Land-reth, but originated with an organization in Ontario. It was later on concentrated in the application by the egg pool. In British Columbia at any rate I know that I can safely say every egg producer is solidly behind this legislation. Not only are they behind it individually, but I am familiar with the local organizations in my district; I have had telegrams from the president of the local cooperative pool in British Columbia and from a great many other officials not only recently but for years, asking that this same legislation be passed. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) is well aware of that fact.
What is the purpose of asking for an increase in the tariff on eggs?
Primarily to keep out at certain periods a flood of American eggs. The legislation would not necessarily raise the price of eggs, but to use the well known expression, it would stabilize the market.
In what way?

To prevent egg producers
being put out of business by a sudden influx of American eggs at the glut period of the year. It has been suggested that the Canadian Council of Agriculture are opposed to this measure and it has been said that they should have been consulted. They had the opportunity to express themselves, and if they did not-
They did express themselves.
Be fair on that point.
Did they put their views forward?

Yes, they did.
Mr. NEIiLL: Well, that was unknown to me. However, supposing they did; we have Mr. Landreth, the newly elected president of the Dominion egg pool on the one hand and we have the Canadian Council of Agriculture on the opposite side of the fence. It seems to me I have heard some of my hon. friends to my left, unless I am again mixing things up,

object to the amount which we give to the Canadian council, saying that it is more or less a personal and autocratic body, and that they have grown aloof-

No, not the Canadian
Council of Agriculture.

Is it not the Council of
Agriculture?

No, the Canadian
Council of Agriculture maintains itself; it does not get a grant.

Did I not hear the hon.
member for Weyiburn (Mr. Young) abject last year?
No; the Canadian Horticultural Council does.

I will take back that feature of it; there is another aspect of the matter with which I wish to deal. The question was asked as to what the importation of eggs had been from the United States. In reply the minister cited the importations for a series of years, and it seemed that they were becoming .less rather than greater; the statement of the minister was no doubt correct. The point is that these eggs do not come in in a year; they come in in a month. In the months of January, February and March, when spring eggs are on the market, they not only come in in such large quantities that they ruin the market, but it is the possibility of bringing them in that shakes the market. It does not matter whether there are twelve or fifty carloads brought in in February, the point is that they are there in unlimited quantities, and the mere fact that they exist and are accessible breaks the price. Consequently the price of our eggs is appreciably lowered. Dealers know that the American price is quoted at say 25 cents, and we know that we -cannot produce eggs at that price. If one carload does not break the price they will bring in fifty or one hundred carloads. There is no doubt a necessity to put some kind of check on the importation to reduce the seasonal glut. The purpose might have been achieved by instituting a seasonal tariff such as was suggested at one time, but it appears that it cannot be done. I must protest at the suggestion that there is not a widespread demand for this legislation, and I make the statement that if business along these lines is continued, and if cheap eggs are imported, the poultry people of British Columbia will be put out of the egg business. We are harrassed with the enormous price we have to pay for wheat. Some years ago

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
hon. members from the prairies with the support of some of the members from British Columbia had the Crowsnest rates readjusted so that they would get a good rate on their wheat.

We are not
asking for duty on wheat.

Did they reciprocate and help us to get a lighter freight rate on the feed for our chickens? No. They got what they wanted and we were put into the discard. The result is that to-day we pay more freight on No. 6 wheat, the inferior rubbish that we have to feed our chickens, to bring it from the prairies to Vancouver than they in the prairies pay on No. 1 wheat, worth three times as much.

I must say that the hon. gentleman, contrary to his custom, is quite unfair to-night. The United Farmers of Alberta in convention assembled by unanimous vote supported the application of the British Columbia farmers for reduced rates on wheat shipped to the coast.

Yes, a few months ago. Did they come to the assistance of British Columbia when that province wanted to make it part of the Crowsnest deal a few years ago? In my opinion that was the time to support it. It is all very well to come along now and express an academic sympathy; I must say we are grateful, but what we wanted was action at that time. There is a Scotch saying that "giff gaff makes guid freends." That is, when you get a favour, give a little in return. We are asking for a return, and we will continue to use their inferior wheat at high prices if we are only allowed a living chance to make something. The farmers in my district are not making fortunes; few of them buy cars; none of them are coming to parliament; they coidd not put up the $200 deposit. I will say that I am only demanding a fair deal for the egg producers of the west.
I wish to correct a wrong impression created by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill)-
Only one?

-in regard to
the Canadian Council of Agriculture not appearing before the tariff board to present the case against the application of the poultry pool. As has been stated, the application was made by Mr. Landreth. A date was set for the hearing, and although Mr. Darby of the Canadian Council of Agriculture appeared, Mr. Landreth did not. A second date was set, and on that occasion Mr. Darby again ap-2419-139i
peared, and Mr. Landreth did not but sent a request for a further adjournment. On the third occasion Mr. Darby travelled all the way from Winnipeg to attend the meeting and again Mr. Landreth did not appear on the scene, but again sent a message asking for a further adjournment. When a date for the hearing was finally set Mr. Darby could not be present. As for the representative of the Consumers' League of Canada, I must say that I happened to be with him on the morning of the hearing. He did not know anything about it until the hearing was about to start, at which time he received a message intimating that his presence was requested.

I wish to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. There was no application from the province of British Columbia when the Crowsnest pass agreement was passed in this house in 1923. For that matter I do not remember that the hon. gentleman himself was very active in the matter. I wish to say that these countervailing duties constitute a vicious feature which has been introduced into the tariff at this time. Bad as the tariff system is, these countervailing duties make it much worse, and they never were asked for by the consumer. The profit derived from them is confined to the dealer exclusively and he is the only person who can possibly benefit. Such a measure is bound to increase the cost of living. I have maintained for a long time that by one stroke of the pen the government can lower the cost of living and improve production both on the farms and in the industries of the country. The policy of the government as shown by these countervailing duties is to make bargains with the dealers and manufacturers, and the cost of living is. going up year by year. It is a mistake to expect that any consumer can benefit by a countervailing duty; it only gives the dealers a chance to charge the home consumer a price that will give him a profit and which will enable him, when the markets are glutted, to ship his goods to any country in the world, at the same time keeping up the price at home high enough to give him a profit for his entire output. I particularly protest against these countervailing duties.
A great many of these items come on foodstuffs alone. Surely if the efficiency of a nation can be measured by anything it is by the extent to which the cost of living is kept down in line with world prices. During the last two or three years our government has done nothing but increase the cost of living to the worker. This does not even help the manufacturer, for the simple reason that

wages must go up; but wages never go up as a countervailing measure against the high cost of the articles on which our manufacturers get a price fixing power. Wages are always behind; they are never high enough to meet the high cost of living in this protective country. Countervailing duties are bound to raise our cost of living another notch this year, and surely it has been high enough in all reason during the years gone by.
I should like to know from the Minister of Finance who asked for these countervailing duties in general. Did the Consumers' League, who has backed him up all these years, ask for them? Only the dealers asked for them, I believe, and it seems to me that only those with whom this government can make a bargain get the advantage in the tariff schedules.

opposite effect and only bring about further difficulties. If this duty was increased for the purpose of preventing the market from being glutted during a certain period of the year, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni suggested, it should only be a seasonal tariff and not one that is in effect all year. As I understand it, this tariff will be in effect twelve months in the year and not during a certain period only, as I understood the hon. member to say he desired. Consequently I do not see that this duty will have any effect; if it does not increase the tariff it is not going to benefit the egg producers in Canada. On the other hand, if the increased tariff is not going to have the effect of keeping out eggs from other countries I do not see what advantage it will be. Personally I would prefer to see the duty remain as it was previously.

If in your opinion it is not

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend from North Winnipeg need worry about the possibility of eggs costing more, because the Canadian hen apparently is a very industrious individual. During the last year for which I have a complete record it produced 272,000,000 dozen eggs, and our total imports during the same iperiod were only 1,000,000 dozen. I am not going to argue the general merits of this proposal, but I do believe that it will be effective in connection with the point which the hon. member for Comox-Allbemi made some time ago with reference to the spring production of eggs in Canada. As a farmer who principally grows wheat I have only an incidental interest in eggs, and a great many hon. members here are in the same position. However, I do not think we should entirely forget that there are farmers, just as much entitled to consideration as such, whose principal source of income is eggs or poultry, and there is no doubt in my mind that the Saskatchewan poultry producers, whose application is here on record, would have repudiated their official publicly if he had been acting in opposition to their wishes in the matter. As a matter of fact the Saskatchewan poultry pool, so-called, made representations to me in this connection, and they do believe rightly or wrongly that during that particular period of the year when everyone is striving for winter egg production a measure such as this will be beneficial to them in preventing their prices from being knocked

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
down to summer levels while they are still on a winter cost basis of production. That really is their argument, and I paid some attention bo it from that point of view.

If the Canadian hen is such
a wonderful producer why does she need any protection against other hens?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Canadian hen
operates according to the course of nature; she does mot lay as freely in the cold weather as she does in the warmth of sjpring. Nature has something to do with all these operations. In the winter she requires more assistance from her owner; she requires more shelter, more careful feeding and a great many other things. If my hon. friend would just go into the poultry business he would learn a lot about it in a very short time.

The point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni with respect to the freight rate on wheat seems to me deserving of some little consideration. When I hear hon. members for British Columbia ask for an increase in the duty on eggs I wonder if what they really want is not a reduction in the freight rate on the wheat which they feed their hens. As a matter of fact to-day the export rate on wheat to Vancouver is only-half the domestic rate. You take a given point in the prairies, with two cars of wheat on the siding. Both these cars are set out at Vancouver; one is used domestically and the wheat is sold to the poultry producers of British Columbia. They pay a rate of 45 cents per 100 pounds, while another car, handled from the same point in the same train, billed for export and sale to Chinamen-probably producing eggs to ship into Canada-bears a rate of 22J cents per 100 pounds, exactly one half. That seems to me to be a very important point. I do not raise any more objection to the duty on eggs than other goods, as I think they are just as much entitled to protection as anything else. However, I do insist that the producer of British Columbia is hampered by the freight rates which he is forced to pay. The Chinaman is able to buy our prairie wheat to feed to his hens, which is delivered at a lower rate, thus putting him in a preferred position to ship his eggs back to Canada. As to opposition being offered by the farmers of the prairie, I can assure my hon. friend that there never was or never will be any opposition to any adjustment of freight rates; he is entirely wrong in that statement.
Not opposition, but just a sort of lukewarmness.
My hon. friend could not expect us to ask for something in his interest; I think the lukewarmness is entirely on the part of the egg producers of British Columbia.
They have not started anything.

If my hon. friend were just as energetic in trying to secure a reduction in the freight rates as he has been to secure an increase in the duty on eggs, I think we would get somewhere. Let him start something and I can assure him that we will all be behind him.

I was not raising that question, but I said that if there were any merit in protection-
Did the hon. member not say that he was entitled to it if anyone was?

I am not arguing the point.
Are you or are you not?

No, he was not.
He voted his judgment.
