I would just like to repeat
what I said yesterday. There is a good deal of talk with regard to alleviating the troubles of the farmers. Every member of the house who has spoken has expressed the view that agriculture is the basic industry of the country and should be assisted as far as possible, but when we come to translating that sentiment into concrete action, I find that agriculture is left entirely alone, especially by hon. gentlemen opposite. They say that they wish to protect agriculture as far as possible. I am here, representing a farming constituency and with some knowledge of what I speak, to say that this particular item of butter is not going to help the farmers I have said before that it will not help them, that it will prove utterly detrimental to the best interests of the farmers in western Canada. I am not
2202	COMMONS
Ways md Means-Customs Tariff
including British Columbia now; I am speaking of the three prairie provinces of which I know something. I am sorry the minister has gone; nevertheless he will read what I have to say in Hansard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He will be
here in a moment.

I said yesterday, and I repeat, that the imposition of a tariff on butter will not affect the producer of butter in western Canada over a period. I showed yesterday that even with the tremendous importation of New Zealand and Australian butter in 1928, there was only one month of the year of 1929 when the importations were less than in 1928. Two months were the same, and the imports in the other months of 1929 were greater. If you take that in conjunction with the importation of 9,5,000 pounds of butter in 1925, the price of 1929 was greater than the price of 1925. I wish to point out to the house that in western Canada to-day there are tremendous troubles affecting all the farmers, and the result is that the farmers are likely to leave the land. I know of men to-day who have been in the country from twenty to thirty years, and who five or ten years ago were wealthy, with money in the bank and in investments, many of whom have had to take mortgages within the last three or four years on their original homesteads; and they were competent farmers, none better on the face of the earth. Yet conditions have placed them in that position.
I wish also to direct attention to this fact. In all the legislation that we are putting through to-day, there is nothing that directly benefits agriculture. We are not giving to agriculture the recognition that we should give and which the house expects. There is little room for doubt in my mind that we will have again the same agitation for farmers' rights unless this house is prepared to do something for them. I am quite sure that the low tariff sentiment wall be revived in the west in the absence of some remedial measures. That sentiment unfortunately has gone into abeyance for the time being and protection has entered into their viewpoint. They saw something more or less tangible immediately before their eyes, and taking the shortsighted view that men sometimes will take, they have grasped at that straw. I say that this tariff on butter is likely to prove most detrimental, for it will destroy absolutely the feeling of the men on the farm which hitherto has been their strength. I care not for the opinions of anyone to the contrary, protection cannot benefit the farmers of western Canada. While we are on

an export basis our prices are ruled by world markets, and we cannot possibly benefit by any system of protection. Yet despite that selfevident fact we see the thin edge of protection being imposed to destroy the efficiency and morale of the farmers. I protest most strenuously against the imposition of this tariff. I give my opinion to the government as sincerely as a man can give it that I think they are making a great mistake. It seems to me that the Minister of Finance should stare the reason why these tariffs are being imposed, and he should also state if it is the intention of the government to carry the policy further into effect.
I do not propose to take the hon. gentleman seriously, Mr. Chairman. He is simply making campaign excuses for his opposition to the subamendment and his support of the budget.

Mr. Chairman, this item is
on the same basis as the protection of eggs. The dairy industry of the prairie provinces has made substantial increase in the production of butter. Last year we increased our production something over 20 per cent, in spite of the fact that perhaps we had the driest year and the greatest scarcity of pasture that I ever remember. If we continue to develop at this rate, I presume we will soon be exporting large quantities of butter, which means that we will be compelled to take world prices for our product. Therefore I am still of the opinion that this item will not benefit the farmer. If we could get some relief in other lines that would reduce our cost of production it would be of real assistance to us. In this connection I desire to read a short paragraph from the report of the annual meeting of the National Dairy Council of Canada held in Toronto, October 18 and 19, 1929. The president Mr. J. A. Caulder said:
A year or two ago when Mr. Stephen and myself were struggling along trying to find some money to buy posters and literature, we went to the other side and we discovered that we could buy posters for about one-quarter to one-half what we could have them made for in this country.
It is a strange condition that we in this country, where we produce more paper and pulp than any other country in the world, cannot furnish posters for advertising purposes as cheaply as they are produced in the United States. I merely quote that as an instance- I might cite others-where a reduction would be appreciated by the farmers of the prairie provinces.

Mr. Chairman, this is indeed a strange spectacle. Here we have hon. mem-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
bers who probably have done more to urge the government to grant low tariffs and reduced rates on the very commodity to which they are referring than any of their colleagues and thus have helped to bring about such a critical situation in the dairy industry that the government itself has been compelled to turn a complete political somersault. Now we have the same members rising in their places to apologize to the indignant farmers who are dissatisfied, but in so doing they are only aggravating the situation. Never in any decade of our history have the agriculturists of this country received such scant recognition and such unfavourable treatment as we have received during the past ten years from this government. There is not a farmer from one end of Canada to the other but realizes that nothing has struck the basic industry of this country so hard as this government's treatment of the very item under discussion.
Nonsense.

I am not an authority on medicine, but 1 think I know as much about dairy farming as the hon. member for Saskatoon. All he has to do to realize the critical condition of our dairy industry is to look at our butter importations during the last couple of years. Every farmer in the province of Ontario who receives a cheque for his cream knows that four weeks ago it represented only 60 per cent of what he was getting in the corresponding period last year.
A lot of Tory propaganda.

Not at all; I am simply stating facts. The reason for this decline is simply the huge importations of New Zealand butter. We have ceased to be an exporting country so far as butter is concerned. When this government came into power we exported millions of pounds of butter to the United States and Great Britain. And what has happened to the cheese market? The Minister of Agriculture and his deputy have sent letters all over the Dominion asking our farmers for some solution of the present agricultural depression. Why? Because we have lost our cheese trade in England to a great extent; we are not exporting half the quantity that we were before the war. Our meat exports to Great Britain have felt the same pinch, having been more or less affected by the decline in the dairy industry. In fact where we used to export $78,000,000 worth to Great Britain, last year we exported only $7,500,000 worth. As to the butter situation, we have simply changed from an exporting country of twenty-five to thirty million pounds
to an importing country of over thirty-four million pounds. At the rate of our present importations we shall probably import fifty million pounds this year. Surely those who have experienced this disastrous condition of affairs should hesitate to-night to rise and condemn this small measure of protection, which, I submit, Mr. Chairman, is not half enough. The request of the dairy council is altogether too modest. A small percentage of our dairymen belong to that organization, simply because the dairy industry has become so demoralized that Ontario farmers who were milking ten, twelve and twenty cows a few years ago, to-day are milking only a sufficient number to provide for their own requirements.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, the situation is critical to-day. Our farms in Ontario are not worth more than 60 per cent of the price they fetched when this government came into power. The people in New Zealand have taken advantage of the free trade doctrines of this government, and their farms have risen in value from $200 or $300 to $500 or $600 an acre.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What country?

New Zealand. I submit you ca^i go on down the line and you will find that because of the action of this government in the past it has had to-day to make a rightabout face. Those members who prompted the United States government to take the action they did take are rising tonight and offering the panacea of low tariff. Mr. Chairman, the greatest criticism which we could offer in connection with this item is that the tariff is not half high enough, because the industry is almost entirely ruined; it will take reestablishment and protection to bring it back to normal.

Before the hon. gentleman
takes his seat I would like to ask him a question. Does he believe that the Canadian dairyman would receive more for his dairy products if he were on an export basis?
When we were on an export basis we did receive more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that is absolutely wrong.
I am right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong; surely he knows better than that.

If my hon. friend will consult the records as to the price of cream three or four weeks ago and compare that price with that which obtained in 1920 he will find that I am correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am speaking of the

world market for butter? There is no such thing as a world market for butter, and there never was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have sold some there, and I think I know as much about it as tije hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.

I wish to point out what would seem to be inconsistencies regarding butter and some other things. Before the Australian treaty went into effect the duty on butter never did the farmer any good. When the Australian treaty was consummated, however, the duty was practically taken off butter from Australia and placed on raisins from other countries. Now we have a duty on butter and the duty on raisins and the result is that the cost of living has been increased. In regard to tea, the duty has been taken off under the British preference, and that no doubt will be welcomed all over the country. If the tariff is a measure used for the purpose of getting revenue it should have been levied on tea and taken off raisins, and the result would have been somewhat easier on the farmer. The duty on butter is not going to benefit the farmer, it will benefit only the merger that is being formed. The farmers' shares in the cooperative company which has been formed throughout the country are being bought by the groups which are trying to form a merger for the distribution of dairy products and the control of the price of the farmer's cream. This will not benefit even the cream producer; it will be a hardship on the consumer, and the price of living will be raised all round.

The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) seems to think that the government has done nothing for the farmer, but I must say he is not in line with the thought expressed in the Montreal Gazette of May 10, 1930. I wish to read an extract from that paper:
Perhaps the Fansher group will inform the house, and the people of the Dominion, what they mean by more effective consideration for agriculture. The prevailing impression has been that in cheapening the so-called instruments of production, in reducing rail rates, and in divers other -ways, the King government has shown far more consideration for agriculture and the agriculturist than for any other industry or any other class; and now there is to be a measure of protection for the farmer against foreign competition. There is something wrong with the Fansher reasoning.
I would remind my hon. friend that the excerpt I have read is from an editorial in the Montreal Gazette.

Does the hon. gentleman
contend that the Montreal Gazette is an expert in agricultural matters?

My hon. friend has condemned the government by saying that it has done nothing for agriculture. I have read from a Conservative newspaper and it clearly admits that the King government has done more for agriculture than it has done for any other industry.
They have done nothing for any other industry.

Hon. members
on this side of the house can see that members of the opposition are pressing for increased protection for the manufacturing industries. The farmers of the country can see that, also. I thought it was wise however to put this editorial on record, because it is an admission by an outstanding Canadian paper that the King government has done more for agriculture than has any previous government.

It is amusing to hear these old free traders trying to square themselves with their constituents, after voting for the budget. I am forced to suggest to the Minister of Finance that we should leave the budget and allow the people of Canada to decide its fate. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite are not going to endeavour to force this budget through the house and not give the people of Canada a chance to decide what they want.
Speak for yourself.

A statement was made to-night 'by the Minister of Finance and contradicted on this side of the bouse, as to the comparative prices of butter in this country

and in the markets of the world. When 1 speak of the world market I refer to the London market. For some years I have studied these prices, and as a matter of fact I have statistics on the subject. I have compiled figures for eight years past showing the comparative prices, week by week, in this country and in London. As a result I must say that in that instance I confirm in every respect the statement of the Minister of Finance that week by week, month by month and year by year for eight years the London price was consistently lower than the Canadian price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And it is to-day.

We have witnessed a remarkable spectacle in this house to-night. The gentlemen on the other side who have just spoken have consistently opposed any increase in the tariff on butter. They spoke against the abrogation of the New Zealand agreement, and last night when, they voted on the budget they voted in favour of the abrogation of that agreement. They voted in favour of higher duties on butter and again to-night they are talking against schedules in the tariff which they supported last might. It seems to me that their constituents will wonder what position these hon. gentlemen are taking. I wonder what will happen if this government ks returned to power; I wonder what will happen to these schedules, in the light of what has been, said across the floor to-night. What are the people of the Dominion of Canada who believe that there should be a duty on butter to think of what we have witnessed this evening. Surely they are going to say that we cannot put any confidence in these men and that very likely, if they should be returned to power, these schedules will be interfered with again very quickly.

Why did my
hon. friend vote against the budget?

I will tell my hon. friend Why
I voted against it; there were several reasons. The first reason is because I have no confidence in this government or in any government supported by men who vote one way one day and talk the other way the next day. The next reason is because although the dairy council only asked for 4 .cents under the British preference I believe that if they thought they had any chance of getting more they would have asked for it. I believe as well that since channels of trade have been established between Canada and New Zealand it is going to take more than 4 cents a pound duty to keep that butter out of this country.
Now I want to say a word in regard to what the Minister of Finance said as to prices
in London and those in Canada. I think what the hon. member to my left said is very largely true, that prices in London have been lower, but we must remember that London is a free trade market. On the other hand, up to this year prices have been higher in United States cities for a great number of years past than they have been either in London or in Canada, and that is a protected market.
I think that is a sufficient answer to the arguments which have been advanced by the Minister of Finance and by the gentleman to my left.
Customs tariff-28a. Tea imported direct from the country of growth and production, and tea purchased in the United Kingdom, when in wrappings, cartons or other packages of not less than five pounds weight each, per pound.
Provided that tea shall be entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff upon evidence satisfactory to the minister that such tea has been produced wholly in- the British dominions, colonies and possessions, and not otherwise: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, 9 cents; general tariff, 10 cents.

I would like to direct the attention of the Minister of Finance to the effect which the proposed tariff on tea will have on the tea dealers. However acceptable free tea may be to the general run of people it does seem unjust to penalize the tea dealers of Canada in order to bring about that condition. I should like to see the Minister of National Revenue here during the discussion of this item, because both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue are concerned in this question, and I would ask the Minister of Finance to take up this matter some other time with the Minister of National Revenue.
I believe a great injustice is threatened to the tea dealers of Canada. In 1918 a duty of 10 per cent was placed on tea under the war Revenue Act in order to meet the exceptional expenditures during and after the war. That was quite understandable, but an unusual and exceptional course was followed after the adoption of that tariff. Authority was given the excise department at the same time to follow the tea that already had been cleared through customs and stored in the tea warehouses and collect upon it that same duty of 10 per cent. I know of no other instance of an article being followed up in this way and an excise tax collected amounting to the duty on the article. It may be that this has occurred before, but I know of no similar instance.
In any event it was a very unusual and exceptional condition. Then on the 1st of May

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
of this year the Minister of Finance announced that he proposed to make tea free. What was the result? It left the tea dealers in the lurch. As usual, their warehouses were stored with tea on which duty had been paid, and if the minister pursues the course which he has indicated, but which I hope he will reconsider, the tea dealers again will be heavy losers. It does seem unjust that both coming and going the tea dealers should be so unfortunate as to receive this treatment from the government. The tea dealers say that not only was the tax that was placed on tea in 1918 followed up by excise to the warehouses, but that to-day they will lose the duty they have already paid on tea in their warehouses. They contend that it is only fair and just that now, when the minister proposed to abolish the tariff, they should be refunded the amount of duty on the tea which is stored in their warehouses. The government should not have that duty under all circumstances, when they are putting it on and again when they are taking it off.
I know it is said that when the duty is taken off an article it is the custom that the dealers who are affected must suffer the loss, but I desire to point out to the minister that the special War Revenue Act was a special measure, that the seeking out of the tea warehouses was an exceptional measure and that therefore it is only fair and reasonable that now the tea dealers should be treated in an exceptional way, if necessary. It is true that the war tax was an unusual measure, but surely that is not a reason for penalizing those who are concerned now. On the contrary, we should endeavour so to meet the situation that the tea dealers concerned should not suffer in this instance. I submit that in this case the tea dealers should not bear the consequences of the government's action; exceptional conditions warrant exceptional treatment.
If the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue ask for a precedent, then I would say that in 1627 a precedent was established for this practice. The minister must not look doubtful, as I rather think he is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

When the tariff was raised on this article the exceptional course was pursued of following the tea to the warehouses and although it had been cleared already by the customs 10 cents per pound was exacted. Now, without warning of any kind, this article is made free of duty and these dealers are undergoing a very serious loss. It is all very well to give the ordinary run of persons the benefit of free tea, but why penalize the tea dealers? The argument against the payment of a refund may be that it would be difficult to accomplish, but that is not sufficient reason for refusing to remedy an injustice. The alternative is to bring this change in tariff into force a certain number of months hence, or if the minister is what I would consider obdurate and is not prepared to be convinced, he could gradually reduce it and make the cut this year one-third or one-half.

The hon. gentleman has been stating that the tea dealers have suffered from the cut of seven cents a pound in the duty on tea. Will he explain why the tea dealers have voluntarily reduced the price of tea by fifteen cents a pound, when the cut in the duty has been only seven cents a pound?

I am not in the tea
trade. I do not say this in a frivolous way, but that is their own business. If they consider that good business; if tljey consider they are going to appeal to their customers on that ground, that is their own affair. But I say
that beyond doubt the tea dealers of this country will suffer heavy loss unless action is taken in the matter.

I explained the amendment some time ago. It is to make sure that the five-pound package falls into one item or the other. The item as amended will read:
Tea imported direct from the country of growth and production, and tea purchased in the United Kingdom, when in wrappings, cartons or other packages of more than five pounds weight.
The other tea item would correspond, so that the package which was exactly five pounds would be in one item or the other.
In reference to what the hon. member for St. John-Albert has had to say regarding the reduction in duty and consequent hardship upon tea dealers, it is always a difficulty in connection with reductions in tariffs that some people may have on hand stocks of the articles concerned which, as a result of the reduction, must be disposed of at lower prices than prevailed before the reduction took place. That is a well known difficulty, I think it is correct to say, in all British countries in relation to the budget. In all British countries the budget items become operative immediately upon the delivery of the budget and business becomes accustomed to that condition. With regard to the previous situation in 1918, when a duty was imposed upon tea by the parliament of that day, my hon. friend says that the dealers then suffered an injustice because the then government decided to impose that tax upon tea which was in stock at the time but which had been cleared from customs. I can hardly follow that argument for the reason that immediately the price of tea is raised, and I have no doubt the stocks of tea upon which that extra duty was paid by the wholesale tea dealers were passed along to the consumer just the same as all that subsequently was dealt with. I do not think they suffered any loss on that occasion and that should not be urged as a reason why special consideration should be extended now. They had every opportunity of passing on to the ultimate consumer whatever they themselves paid.
With reference to the present case, I may say that the government has had representations from tea dealers throughout the whole country regarding this question. On the matter of principle, of course my hon. friend is quite right when he states that it is not

I do not want to hold out any hope to my hon. friend that the usual procedure will be departed from, but we are gathering the information. May I point out to him one difficulty?
